title: IAM Policy
summary: An IAM policy is a structured document that grants or denies permissions to a principal in a cloud platform, evaluated by the provider's authorisation engine on every API call. Policies typically bind a principal, an action or set of actions on a resource, and optional conditions such as source address, time, tags or whether multi-factor authentication was used, with an explicit effect of allow or deny. Cloud authorisation is generally default-deny, so access exists only where a policy grants it, and an explicit deny usually overrides any allow. Policies attach at several levels, including identity-based policies on users, groups and roles, resource-based policies on the target itself such as a bucket or key, permission boundaries, session policies and service control policies in an organisation hierarchy, which means the effective permission set is the intersection and union of several documents rather than any single one. Security professionals care because over-permissive policies are a leading cause of cloud compromise and because policy errors are invisible until an attacker or an auditor exercises them. Practical work includes least-privilege scoping, wildcard elimination, analysing cross-account trust relationships, reviewing role assumption chains, and detecting privilege escalation paths where one grant lets a principal modify a policy that grants more. Reviewing the effective permission of a principal, not the intent of a single document, is the discipline the topic teaches.
objectives: You will be able to read a JSON IAM policy and state precisely which principals, actions and resources it authorises.
You will be able to compute the effective permissions of a principal across identity, resource, boundary and organisation policies.
You will be able to identify privilege escalation paths created by policy modification rights.
You will be able to rewrite an over-permissive policy into a least-privilege form and justify each retained grant.
You will be able to explain how condition keys and explicit deny change authorisation outcomes.
You will be able to triage IAM-related alerts such as role assumption anomalies and policy change events.
